item.title: Air India cancels Saudi Arabia flights till Oct 20 after Indian national killed in Houthi attacks: What flyers must know
item.description: Air India cancelled all its flight to and from Saudi Arabia till October 20, amid repeated Houthi attacks on the Middle-East country's airports.
item.dc:creator: Akriti Anand
item.content:encoded: India's national carrier Air India cancelled all its flight to and from Saudi Arabia till October 20, amid repeated Houthi attacks on the Middle-East country's airports.In a travel advisory posted on X on Friday, the airline said all Air India flights to and from Riyadh, Dammam and Jeddah stand cancelled until October 20, 2026."In view of the evolving situation in Saudi Arabia, all Air India flights to and from Riyadh, Dammam and Jeddah stand cancelled until 20 October 2026," Air India posted on X.The airline added, “We are closely monitoring developments and continuously assessing the situation to ensure the safe resumption of operations.”Will flyers get full refund?Air India also informed thar passengers affected by these cancellations are being offered a full refund."At Air India, the safety and security of our passengers and crew remain the highest priority," Air India's X post read.What flyers seeking ‘urgent departure’ from Saudi Arabia must do?Earlier, the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia had said, “Indian nationals requiring urgent departure from Saudi Arabia may consider flights from neighbouring countries, including Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar. However, the concerned individual/s would be responsible for obtaining the necessary visas to enter these countries.” Which other airline announced cancellations? The latest extension by Air India follows earlier flight suspensions announced by Indian carriers IndiGo and Akasa Air amid escalating security concerns in the Middle East. IndiGo, on Thursday, announced extending the cancellation of flights to Saudi Arabia till October 24. On Thursday, Akasa Air said that in view of the prevailing security situation in the Middle East, it has extended the suspension of all flights to and from Riyadh until October 24 and Jeddah until October 21. Why are flights to Saudi Arabia being cancelled? The cancellation of flights come in the backdrop of drone and missile attacks targeting civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthis. The Riyadh airport has also come under multiple attacks as tensions escalated in recent days. The flight disruptions come amid reports of attacks on Saudi aviation infrastructure and heightened security concerns affecting air travel in the region. On Thursday, CCTV footage of the attack Abha International Airport emerged. The clip showed people reacting to an attack on Abha International Airport, in Abha, Asir Province, Saudi Arabia. The Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen said at a press conference on Thursday that Houthi attacks on Abha airport, in southwestern Saudi Arabia near the Yemeni border, had killed three people and wounded 28. The coalition reportedly said the Houthis had launched 20 attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh this month, killing 17 people and wounding 333 others, Reuters reported. The airport, one of Saudi Arabia's main international aviation hubs, was among the civilian infrastructure targeted in what the coalition described as a series of attacks. One Indian killed Meanwhile, the death toll from the October 10 attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh rose to 13 after the Indian Embassy in Riyadh confirmed the death of an Indian national who had been injured in the incident. In a video message to the Indian community shared on the official X handle of the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia, Ambassador Vipul said one Indian national was killed and 11 others were injured in the attack on Riyadh airport on October 10. “There were also 11 other Indians who were injured in the attack, and we are again in touch with the hospital authorities as well as the families to provide all help to them,” he said.Amid the military escalation, the Houthis issued a broad warning to international airlines, foreign workers and commercial travellers to avoid Saudi aviation hubs. The group declared Saudi airspace unsafe, with an explicit exception for the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.Earlier, the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Council strongly condemned the attacks on civilian airports, aircraft and aviation infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, expressing solidarity with the country's government and people.

item.title: Russia-Ukraine war: When Elon Musk shutdown Starlink in 2022, drones went dark — how much power does SpaceX boss hold?
item.description: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy recently claimed that Kyiv's restricted access to Starlink led to civilian deaths because Ukrainian interceptors using the technology could no longer knock down Russian drones as effectively.
item.dc:creator: Akriti Anand
item.content:encoded: Several Ukrainian officials recently alleged that SpaceX abruptly restricted its "military-grade" Starlink services that Ukraine used on the battlefield against Russia. Sources told Axios that the disruptions were observed late Tuesday, but they were restored later. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv's limited access to Starlink led to civilian deaths because Ukrainian interceptors using the technology could no longer knock down Russian drones as effectively. In response to reports, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk highlighted the difference between Starlink and Starshield services, sparking confusion over whether the US government or SpaceX restricted access in Ukraine. Starshield is a militarised version of Starlink that has become a key component of Ukraine’s war in Russia. Starlink provides commercial services, while Starshield is designed for government and national security missions and provides secure communications with higher levels of encryption. Starshield, however, relies on the broader Starlink network. Musk’s comments on X sought to shift responsibility away from his company by only referring to Starshield as the US government-owned hardware. Axios quoted sources as saying that both SpaceX-owned Starlink and 'US-controlled' Starshield services for Ukraine were disrupted this week. There was no confirmation from Musk or the US government on whether they deliberately restricted access. While the system has since been restored, it remains unclear who made the call and why. The decision ignited a firestorm over who controls access to the technology on the front lines of Ukraine, with Ukrainian officials placing the blame on both Musk and President Donald Trump’s administration. Not the first time This wasn't the first time Ukraine's access to the Starlink system was restricted during the war with Russia that began in February 2022. The first known instance of the billionaire actively shutting off Starlink coverage over a battlefield during the conflict was in September 2022, Reuters had said in its special report What happened in 2022? In late September 2022, during a pivotal push by Ukraine to retake territory from Russia, Elon Musk reportedly gave an order that disrupted Ukraine's counteroffensive and dented Kyiv’s trust in Starlink. SpaceX started providing the satellite internet service early in the war to help Ukraine’s military maintain battlefield connectivity. While Musk's company didn't confirm the claim, sources told Reuters that Musk had told a senior engineer at SpaceX's California offices to cut coverage in areas including Kherson, a strategic region north of the Black Sea that Ukraine was trying to reclaim. Staffers complied, the three people told Reuters, deactivating at least a hundred Starlink terminals, their hexagon-shaped cells going dark on an internal map of the company’s coverage. The move also affected other areas seized by Russia, including some of Donetsk province further east. What impact did it have on Ukraine's operation in the battlefield? After Musk’s order, Starlink failure was experienced near the front lines of the war. Ukrainian troops suddenly faced a communications blackout, according to a Ukrainian military official, an advisor to the armed forces, and two others who experienced the failure. Soldiers panicked, drones surveilling Russian forces went dark, and long-range artillery units, reliant on Starlink to aim their fire, struggled to hit targets, according to Reuters' special report. As a result, the Ukrainian military official and the military advisor said that troops failed to surround a Russian position in the town of Beryslav, east of Kherson, the administrative center of the region of the same name. “The encirclement stalled entirely,” said the military official in an interview. “It failed.” Ultimately, Ukraine’s counteroffensive succeeded in reclaiming Beryslav, the city of Kherson and some additional territory Russia had occupied. According to the report, panicked calls by Ukrainian officials during the outage to seek information from Pentagon counterparts were met with few explanations for what could have caused it, five people familiar with the incident said. What prompted Musk's 'order'? It wasn’t clear what prompted Musk’s command, when exactly he gave it, or precisely how long the outage lasted. Three people familiar with the order told Reuters that they believed it stemmed from concerns Musk expressed later that Ukrainian advances could provoke nuclear retaliation from Russia. One of the people was quoted as saying that the shutoff transpired on September 30, 2022. The two others said it was around then, but didn’t recall the exact date. Some senior US officials shared Musk’s concerns that Russia would make good on threats to escalate, one former White House staffer told Reuters. What did Musk, SpaceX say on 2022 incident? The account of the command countered Musk’s narrative of how he has handled Starlink service in Ukraine amid the war. As recently as March that year, in a post on X, his social media site, Musk wrote: “We would never do such a thing.” Musk and Nicolls didn’t respond to requests from Reuters for comment. The US Department of Defense declined to comment. Reuters couldn’t determine whether White House or Pentagon officials after the shutdown had any exchanges with Musk over the outage. A SpaceX spokesperson said by email to Reuters that the news agency’s reporting is “inaccurate” and referred reporters to an X post earlier this year in which the company said: “Starlink is fully committed to providing service to Ukraine.” The spokesperson didn’t specify any inaccuracies in this report or answer a lengthy list of questions regarding the incident, Starlink’s role in the Ukraine war, or other details regarding its business. In 2023, SpaceX had said that it had taken unspecified steps to prevent Ukraine from using Starlink for certain activities, including drone attacks. “Our intent was never to have them use it for offensive purposes,” Gwynne Shotwell, the company’s president, said at a conference in Washington in February of that year. “There are things that we can do, and have done” to prevent it, she added, without providing further detail. Starlink still provides service to Ukraine which is heavily reliant on thousands of SpaceX's Starlink terminals for battlefield communications and some drone operations, as they have proved resistant to espionage and signal jamming throughout the three and a half years of fighting Russia's invasion. Starlink does not operate in Russia. But Ukrainian officials have said that Moscow's troops are also widely using the systems on the frontlines in Ukraine. The 2025 incident Starlink had experienced one of its biggest international outages in July 2025. A senior commander has told Reuters that Starlink systems used by Ukrainian military units were down for two and a half hours overnight. The outage was part of a global issue that disrupted the satellite internet provider. "Starlink is down across the entire front," Robert Brovdi, the commander of Ukraine's drone forces, had said on Telegram in 2025. Musk’s dominance in military affairs: Can he influence conflict in Ukraine? The Reuters report noted that Musk’s sway in military affairs in Washington and beyond – through Starlink’s dominance in satellite communications and SpaceX’s clout in space launches – has reached a dimension previously limited to sovereign governments, alarming some regulators and lawmakers. Musk’s "order" affecting Kherson raised concerns about his ability to influence the conflict in Ukraine. It shocked some Starlink employees and effectively reshaped the front line of the fighting, enabling Musk to take “the outcome of a war into his own hands,” another one of the three people said. Meanwhile, Martha Lane Fox, a member of Britain’s upper house of parliament, said during a debate earlier in 2025, “Elon Musk’s current global dominance exemplifies the dangers of concentrated power in unregulated domains." The parliamentarian is a businesswoman and former board member at Twitter, the social media site that Musk acquired in 2022 and rebranded as X. “Its control,” Lane Fox said of Starlink, “rests solely with Musk, allowing his whims to dictate access to vital infrastructure.” Musk blocked Starlink services in Crimea? The Kherson episode is distinct from an earlier report of an incident that purportedly occurred that same September, involving Crimea just to the south. In his 2023 biography of Musk, author Walter Isaacson reported that the tycoon had ordered Starlink to disable coverage in Crimea, which Russia had annexed from Ukraine after a 2014 invasion that the international community condemned as illegal. Musk, Isaacson wrote, believed a planned Ukrainian attack on Russian vessels in the Crimean port of Sevastopol could prompt nuclear retaliation. After the book was published, Musk denied a shutdown, saying that there had never been coverage in Crimea to begin with. The SpaceX boss had said he had, rather, rejected a Ukrainian request to provide service ahead of Kyiv’s planned attack. Isaacson later conceded his account was flawed. A spokesperson at Isaacson’s publisher declined to comment or make him available for an interview.
